subject: chemistry
title: Planning your practical investigation and poster

scenes.heading: Planning your practical investigation and poster
scenes.say: In Unit 4 you design your own investigation on sustainable energy or materials, then present it as a scientific poster.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Test new boots with the same ball, same kicker, same weather
scenes.science: Change only the independent variable; control the rest
scenes.breaks: you can see the wind outside, but things like heat lost to the air are harder to notice and control.
scenes.say: To test whether new boots help you kick further, you'd use the same ball, the same kicker and the same weather. The boots are the independent variable, the distance is the dependent variable, and everything else is controlled. That makes the test valid.

scenes.heading: Planning your investigation
scenes.say: Start with a specific, testable research question. Write a hypothesis: if this changes, then that will change, because of a chemistry reason. Identify your variables, write a detailed method with a risk assessment using safety data sheets, and keep a logbook throughout.

scenes.heading: Accuracy vs precision
scenes.say: Accuracy is how close you are to the true value. Precision is how close your repeats are to each other. Think of shooting hoops: a tight group of shots all hitting the left of the rim is precise, but not accurate.

scenes.heading: Random vs systematic errors
scenes.say: Random errors scatter readings, like a wobbly bathroom scale, so repeat and average. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way, like a scale that was never zeroed, so fix the method. Spills are mistakes: just redo the trial.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: 0.50 g of ethanol heats 100 g of water by 25.0 °C. Data book value: 29.6 kJ g⁻¹. Find kJ g⁻¹ and the error type.
lines: Heat loss: systematic. Insulate the can.
scenes.say: The water gains ten point four five kilojoules, so that's twenty-one kilojoules per gram, well below twenty-nine point six. Heat lost to the air makes every result too low, so it's a systematic error. Insulate the can and use a draught shield.
scenes.caption: The water gains 10.45 kJ, so that's 21 kJ g⁻¹, well below 29.6. Heat lost to the air makes every result too low, so it's a systematic error. Insulate the can and use a draught shield.

scenes.heading: Your scientific poster
points: About 600 words: let graphs do the talking
scenes.say: Your poster uses the VCAA headings: title, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references. It's about six hundred words, so keep sentences short and let clear, labelled graphs do the talking. Check your teacher's instructions for the details.

points: I change it; it depends; I control the rest
scenes.say: Quick recap. Know your variables. Write if, then, because. Random errors need repeats; systematic errors need a better method. And say your hypothesis is supported, never proven. Now try the practice questions!
